clues.title: Google car: Gen 4 for all car coverage
text: All car coverage in Germany was taken with a **Generation 4** camera.
NOTE: There are some Generation 2 and 3 trekkers, and spill coverage with older dates.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: All car coverage is the Gen 4 camera. There are some older Gen 2 and 3 trekkers and older spill coverage.

clues.title: Bollard: black and white, white-grey reflector
text: Germany uses these **black** and **white** bollards, with white and light-grey reflectors. The reflector will be [orange](https://maps.app.goo.gl/anxpwSBiE6Jfcntr5) on bollards next to intersections.** **They sometimes have plates containing the road number, and potentially other useful information. Many bollards also feature blue attachments on the side.

NOTE: Many European countries have similar bollards, however most will have different coloured reflectors. [Luxembourg](https://maps.app.goo.gl/zK9RvWWR1d1NcnoS9) uses almost identical bollards, but they have 3 bolts instead of 2 on the reflector.

images.caption: Wedge bollards; the red circle zooms in on the road-number plate on the post at the right, with the arrow pointing to it
German wedge bollard: F = front with a rectangular reflector (arrows marked 2), B = back
Wedge bollard: left shot is the back with two round reflectors, F = front with arrows and 3 marking its reflector

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Black and white bollards with white and light-grey reflectors, orange next to intersections. They may have road number plates and blue side attachments. Luxembourg's are almost identical but have 3 bolts on the reflector instead of 2.

clues.title: Language: Ä Ö Ü and ß
text: The official language of Germany is **German**. The German language uses the special letters Ä, Ö, Ü and ß.

NOTE: The other majority German-speaking countries with coverage are Switzerland, Austria and Liechtenstein. In addition, German is spoken in [East Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German-speaking_Community_of_Belgium) and the Italian province of [South Tyrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Tyrol).

images.caption: German text sample with Ä Ö Ü ß shown large

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: German uses the letters Ä, Ö, Ü and ß. Switzerland, Austria and Liechtenstein also speak it, as do East Belgium and South Tyrol.

clues.title: Pole: white rectangular sticker on wood
text: Most wooden poles in Germany will feature a rectangular** white sticker**.

images.caption: A red circle marks a small white sticker on the pole

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Most wooden poles carry a white rectangular sticker.

clues.title: Pole: many pole tops, bar or triangle or T
text: Germany has a wide variety of different poles and pole tops. The most common pole tops being the [horizontal bar with uneven hanging insulators](https://goo.gl/maps/wkQ8ZgBCxShM7vyo6), [Triangle pole top](https://goo.gl/maps/g6rN1vXFzec8cEt8A), and all kinds of [T-shaped pole tops](https://goo.gl/maps/3efen5ZJh2iaVUvi7), which can have varying insulator setups.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A wide variety of poles. Common tops are a horizontal bar with uneven hanging insulators, a triangle, and many T-shaped tops.

clues.title: Sign: black or dark grey sign backs
text: Germany also has a wide variety of sign backs. Notably, you can commonly find **black** or **dark grey** sign backs, which are rather rare in Europe. Most signs will also feature this sticker, with an upside-down red triangle on a black rectangle.
NOTE: Italy, Romania and Albania also have black sign backs, however landscape should be sufficient to tell them apart.

images.caption: Back of a yield sign with a red circle around the sticker on it, left

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A wide variety of sign backs, notably black or dark grey ones, which are rare in Europe. Most carry a sticker with an upside-down red triangle on a black rectangle. Italy, Romania and Albania have black backs too.

clues.title: Bus stop: big yellow and green H
text: Like Austria, Germany uses a wide variety of regional bus stops, all of which have the big **yellow** and **green** **H** symbol on them.

images.caption: German bus stop signs with a big yellow and green H

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Many regional bus stop designs, all with a big yellow and green H. Austria does the same.

clues.title: Mailbox: bright yellow with black logo
text: Mailboxes in Germany are **bright yellow**, and feature this black logo.

images.caption: Bright yellow German mailboxes with a black post horn logo

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Bright yellow mailboxes with a black logo.

clues.title: Bollard: one every 50 metres
text: You will find an excessive amount of bollards on most roads in Germany. Around every 50 metres to be exact.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: An excessive number of bollards on most roads, about every 50 metres.

clues.title: Sign: yellow town entry with metal frame
text: German town entry signs are **yellow** with black text and have a **metallic frame**.
NOTE: These signs can include a lot of useful information too:
- !!The town and/or city name on the top.
- !!The Municipality in the middle.
- !!And the county on the bottom.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Yellow town entry signs with black text and a metal frame. They show the town on top, the municipality in the middle and the county at the bottom.

clues.title: Route marker: blue autobahn km marker
text: Germany uses these** blue** rectangular kilometre markers with a white border for A-Roads (Autobahn). B-Roads and local roads have [white](https://maps.app.goo.gl/L2ViHxRf932m3bGR6) markers with a black border.
NOTE: On smaller roads, you will also see [triangular](https://goo.gl/maps/6TL7zau8sXJ983gq6) markers. See Step 2 below to get acquainted with the regional differences.

images.caption: German km markers: blue Autobahn marker (left) and white B-road marker (right)

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Blue rectangular km markers with a white border are on motorways. Other roads have white markers with a black border, and small roads triangular ones.

clues.title: Sign: pedestrian sign with 5 stripes and a belt
text: German pedestrian signs have **five stripes** and the person has a **belt**.
NOTE: The same design is used in Luxembourg.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Pedestrian signs have five stripes and the person wears a belt. Luxembourg uses the same design.

clues.title: Sign: one-way sign saying Einbahnstraße
text: These one-way traffic signs, with the word ‘**Einbahnstraße**’ written on them, are unique to Germany.
NOTE: In Austria, there will be “EINBAHN” written on the sign.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: One-way signs with the full word 'Einbahnstraße' are unique. Austria's say just 'EINBAHN'.

clues.title: Sign: no stopping signs with white arrows
text: “No Stopping” and “No Waiting” signs in Germany will often have **white arrows** drawn on them.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: 'No Stopping' and 'No Waiting' signs often have white arrows drawn on them.

clues.title: Car: round sticker on windscreen, usually green
text: Circular stickers, that are usually green, are found on the bottom right of the windshield on almost every car in Germany. Not as useful to know, but they will have the number 4 written on them. They can rarely be yellow or red instead, and will have the numbers 3 and 2 respectively.

images.caption: A round green sticker on a car windscreen; the red circle zooms in on it

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Almost every car has a round, usually green sticker at the bottom right of the windscreen with a 4 on it. Rarely yellow (3) or red (2).

clues.title: Landmark: wind turbines everywhere
text: **Wind turbines** are far more common throughout Germany than in any other European country.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Wind turbines are much more common than in any other European country.

clues.title: Landscape: flat north, hilly middle, Alps south
text: Using the surrounding elevation can be crucial for getting good guesses in Germany. Here are some general rules:
- The north and especially northwest is very flat.
- Central Germany is hilly.
- Very southern Germany has big mountains.
Also note that despite having a higher elevation, many parts of southern Germany can still be flat.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The north, especially the northwest, is very flat. The centre is hilly, and the far south has big mountains, though many southern parts are flat despite being high.

clues.title: Postal codes: counter-clockwise from 0 to 9
text: **Postal codes** are arranged in a counter-clockwise fashion, starting with 0 around Saxony and ending with 9 in northern Bavaria and parts of Thuringia.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Postal codes run counter-clockwise, from 0 around Saxony to 9 in northern Bavaria and parts of Thuringia.

clues.title: Flags: each state has its own
text: Each German state has their own flag. Many of them are rare to find, though.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Each state has its own flag, but many are rare to find.

clues.title: Plate: state coat of arms on unblurred plates
text: Each German state also has their own coat of arms. They are found on unblurred licence plates and some official buildings.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Each state has its own coat of arms, seen on unblurred plates and some official buildings.

clues.title: Town names: -ow and -itz east, -weiler and -ach south
text: These are some of the more useful and common place name suffixes. Due to their Slavic origins, endings like **-ow** and **-itz** are primarily found in the east, whereas place names ending in **-weiler** and **-ach** are mainly located in the southern half.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Useful place name endings. Slavic-origin -ow and -itz are mainly in the east, while -weiler and -ach are mainly in the southern half.

clues.title: Guardrail: B-type mostly, A-type in the west
text: While most of Germany uses **B-Type** guardrails, A-type guardrails are common in the northwest, as well as in Rhineland-Palatinate and parts of Bavaria.
NOTE: There will always be rare exceptions. For a good overview of European guardrails, see [this infographic](/images/germany/europeguardrail.png).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Most of the country uses B-type guardrails, but A-type is common in the northwest, in Rhineland-Palatinate and parts of Bavaria. Exceptions always exist.

clues.title: Sign: bike direction signs, green or red text
text: **Bicycle direction signs** typically feature a white background with green lettering. In Hamburg, North Rhine-Westphalia and a neighbouring part of Lower Saxony, you will instead find red lettering. The Saarland has its own distinctive design, with white text on a dark green background.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Bicycle direction signs are white with green text. In Hamburg, North Rhine-Westphalia and a nearby part of Lower Saxony the text is red. Saarland has white text on dark green.

clues.title: Sign: street sign backs, folded or flat
text: You can use the backs of street signs to regionguess Germany.
Here are examples of a [folded](https://goo.gl/maps/edxgzquC6mXrySvh9), and [flat](https://goo.gl/maps/5cw4KiWCdgYQXFzy7) sign back.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Backs of street signs help to guess the region. Examples show a folded and a flat back.

clues.title: Sign: street sign back connectors
text: You can also use the sign back connectors on street signs to regionguess Germany.
NOTE: The double connector on triangular signs are generally [wider](https://goo.gl/maps/zNwkDqQkt5vCVAGx7). T-shaped connectors may look like [this](https://goo.gl/maps/ru72EcB1fE3dt8zZA).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The connectors on street sign backs also help with the region. Double connectors on triangular signs are usually wider, and T-shaped connectors exist.

clues.title: Landscape: the only high mountains, Austrian border
text: The German Alps is the most mountainous region in Germany, it is mostly concentrated on the Austrian Border.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The Alps are the most mountainous region, mostly along the Austrian border.

clues.title: Plants: Scots pine with orange trunks, northeast
text: Baltic Pines or [Pinus sylvestris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinus_sylvestris) are generally more concentrated in the **northeast** of Germany. They can be recognized by their orange-tinged trunk.
NOTE: This map is very approximate.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Scots pines, with orange-tinged trunks, are mostly in the northeast. The map is approximate.

clues.title: Trees: white paint near the base, northeast
text: You can spot trees that are painted white close to the bottom of the trunk in the northeast.
NOTE: You will rarely find them outside the shaded region.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Trees painted white near the bottom of the trunk are in the northeast, rarely outside.

clues.title: Landscape: flat farmland with a ridge to the NE
text: The flat plains southeast of **Regensburg** can be recognised by the **slight ridge** often visible to the northeast. The plains themselves are **flat**, and quite **agricultural**.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The flat plains southeast of Regensburg are very agricultural, often with a slight ridge to the northeast.

clues.title: Plants: vineyards, mostly southwest
text: Vineyards are mostly concentrated in the **southwest** of Germany. However, there are a couple regions further east as well.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Vineyards are mostly in the southwest, with a few more regions further east (Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt border, Elbe in Saxony). There are 13 wine regions.

clues.title: Plants: hop fields
text: You can find [hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hops) fields in these regions. They are commonly seen just north of Munich.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Hop fields are common just north of Munich, mainly between Ingolstadt and Landshut, with minor areas in the east.

clues.title: Houses: brick houses in the northwest
text: These brick houses are generally concentrated in **northwestern** Germany.
NOTE: This map is very approximate.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Brick houses are mostly in the northwest. The map is approximate.

clues.title: Houses: thatched roofs, rock walls, north coast
text: **Thatched roofs** and **rock walls** are most common on the [North Frisian Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Frisian_Islands), as well as mainland Schleswig-Holstein. You can also commonly find them in coastal **resort towns** in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Thatched roofs and stone walls are most common on the North Frisian Islands and the northern mainland coast, and in coastal resort towns in the northeast.

clues.title: Houses: black slate walls like fish scales
text: Houses with **black slate walls**, resembling fish scales, are commonly found in a large area of central Germany.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Houses with black slate walls that look like fish scales are common over a large area of central Germany.

clues.title: Houses: big socialist-era apartment blocks
text: These **large**, utilitarian **apartment buildings** constructed during the socialist era, that are also known as “[Commie blocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_planning_in_communist_countries)” are common in all of former East Germany.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Large, plain apartment blocks from the socialist era are common across the former East.

clues.title: Bollard: green cap on top in the west
text: Some bollards in North Rhine-Westphalia have a **green** bit at the top. The top can also be [another colour](https://goo.gl/maps/U6GkPR5z4NMDGqZc6).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Some bollards in North Rhine-Westphalia have a green top, sometimes another colour.

clues.title: Bollard: green cap with 'LVR' and coat of arms
text: Some of the green caps will have the text ‘**LVR**’, along with a small **coat of arms**. These specific green caps are unique to southern North Rhine-Westphalia.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Some green caps carry the text LVR and a small coat of arms, unique to the southern part of North Rhine-Westphalia.

clues.title: Bollard: round wooden with painted top
text: These **round wooden** bollards, which have a painted top, are found in Bavaria.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Round wooden bollards with a painted top are found in Bavaria.

clues.title: Bollard: irregular, no white lower half
text: These irregular looking bollards, which do not have a white encasing on the bottom half, are found on K-roads in this region of **Lower Saxony**. K-Roads in this region will not have any other type of bollard.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Odd bollards without a white lower half are on K-roads in a part of Lower Saxony. K-roads there have no other bollard type.

clues.title: Bollard: simple orange posts
text: These **simple orange posts** are most commonly found in Bavaria, and also in the other highlighted states.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Simple orange posts are most common in Bavaria and a few other highlighted states.

clues.title: Trees: tiny green tags
text: Many trees in Brandenburg and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern have these **tiny green markers** on them. You can very rarely find them in Lower Saxony.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Many trees in the northeast (Brandenburg and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern) have tiny green markers. Very rarely in Lower Saxony.

clues.title: Route marker: white, split by black lines in three
text: Bavaria uses these white rectangular road markers, which are divided by black lines into **three sections**. The left section provides the road you are currently on.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Bavaria's white rectangular markers are divided by black lines into three sections. The left section shows the road you're on.

clues.title: Route marker: simple rectangle with rounded corners
text: You can find these simple **rectangular** markers, with **rounded edges** in Lower Saxony.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Simple rectangular markers with rounded edges are in Lower Saxony.

clues.title: Route marker: metal border around the marker
text: These markers with a **metallic border** around the marker itself are found in Schleswig-Holstein and Lower Saxony.
NOTE: The numbers after the comma are usually smaller on the markers in Lower Saxony.

images.caption: German route markers compared: Schleswig-Holstein (top row) and Lower Saxony (bottom row)

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Markers with a metal border are in Schleswig-Holstein and Lower Saxony. The numbers after the comma are usually smaller in Lower Saxony.

clues.title: Bollard: triangular posts by region
text: These **triangular** posts are commonly found in these regions.
You can go more in-depth with them, too.
- Rhineland-Palatinate and Saxony use unpainted, rocky-looking posts, with white plates stuck on each side.
- Saarland, Thuringia, and Baden-Württemberg use white posts, with the same white plates attached. The posts are usually quite tall, except in Baden-Württemberg, where shorter ones are used.
- Baden-Württemberg also uses grey posts.
- North Rhine-Westphalia uses white posts without white plates on the sides. You can also find posts which go all the way to the ground.
- Hesse barely uses these posts at all. However, when they do, it is quite unpredictable.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Triangular posts vary by state. Rhineland-Palatinate and Saxony have unpainted rocky-looking posts with white plates. Saarland, Thuringia and Baden-Württemberg have white posts with white plates (shorter in BW), and BW also has grey ones. North Rhine-Westphalia has white posts without plates.

text: Bollards standing on these **black disks** are commonly found in all of **eastern** Germany.

images.caption: Bollard standing on a black disk at its base, circled in red

clues.title: Street sign: city-by-city designs
text: - [Berlin](https://goo.gl/maps/byoGqSgok1uhmjCy6) uses white signs with a grey border, and a separate section for numbers under the street name. Also note how the letter ß looks.
- [Munich](https://goo.gl/maps/RMshmDUSNucokmWN9) has blue street signs with a white decorative border that does not touch the corners. Also note the unique font.
- [Stuttgart](https://goo.gl/maps/fPFeuNukTiRTWoki7) uses **black** signs without a border.
- [Düsseldorf](https://goo.gl/maps/L9kbaYYwzV2iFE9n9) has **black** signs with a white border, similar to Munich. The signs have a **metallic frame.**
- [Dortmund](https://goo.gl/maps/3PhsxrNkq7oduns59) uses blue signs with a white border and a grey frame. The signs also have a separate section for numbers under the street name.
- [Essen](https://goo.gl/maps/wXngUHVBa2eS9CH2A) has blue signs with a very **thick** metallic frame.
- [Dresden](https://goo.gl/maps/S83P48x1grRfYR8H8) has blue signs with a unique font.
- [Hanover](https://goo.gl/maps/4oWah3dfDGep5sR6A) uses white signs with a **wider** than usual gap between the sign and metallic frame.
- [Nuremberg](https://goo.gl/maps/fUp3W4uEMsbFGtYH6) has blue signs with a unique font. The signs also have a grey frame with a small gap between it and the sign.
- [Wuppertal](https://goo.gl/maps/SUe7ExCD7S7SJDye7) uses white signs with a unique font and a white painted frame with a small gap between it and the sign.
- [Mainz](https://goo.gl/maps/bj8Mt4jAxn9duXodA) has a mix of blue signs, and this unique **red** variant.
- [Frankfurt ](https://goo.gl/maps/FDzr8ZLrSehrSAoC8)uses blue street signs with a metallic border around the sign, as well as the separate section for numbers under the street name.
NOTE: More rarely, some smaller towns can use similar signs to those in this graphic.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Big cities have their own street signs: Berlin white with a grey border and a number box, Munich blue with a decorative white border, Stuttgart black without border, Düsseldorf black with white border and metal frame, Dortmund, Essen, Dresden, Nuremberg and Frankfurt blue variants, Hanover and Wu…

clues.title: Language: Slavic Sorbian near Poland and Czech border
text: [Sorbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorbian_languages), a **Slavic** language, is spoken near the Polish and Czech border. You can find it on a variety of signs in these regions.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Sorbian, a Slavic language, appears on various signs near the Polish and Czech borders.

clues.title: Bus stop: each city state has its own
text: Every city state uses a unique and recognisable bus stop.
- Berlin uses **segmented** bus stops, with a **yellow** signpost.
- Hamburg bus stops have a **red signpost**, and the route numbers are within **hexagons**. Note that they can be found outside of Hamburg as well.
- Bremen proper uses simple bus stops, which have the bus stop name within a **red section**. The edges can be rounded.
- Bremerhaven, which is still part of Bremen, uses bus stops with a **grey section** on the opposite side of the signpost. And the bus stop name is **red** within a **yellow** section.

clues.summary: Berlin: segmented stops on a yellow post. Hamburg: red post with route numbers in hexagons. Bremen: simple stops with the name in a red section. Bremerhaven: grey section on the back of the post and the name in red on yellow.
